newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Midopa takeover bid far from over-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Midopa takeover bid far from over-analysts.

text.p: South Korea's Shindongbang Corp has thrown down a gauntlet to the country's industrial conglomerates by going ahead with a bid to take over a leading retailer, analysts said on Thursday.

Shindongbang, the nation's largest edible oil company, is pressing on with its bid for Midopa Department Store despite opposition from a business lobbying group, the Federation of Korean Industries, which is opposed to a hostile takeover.
Shindongbang told the Korea Stock Exchange late on Wednesday it had filed a court application to block an attempt by Midopa to defend itself against a corporate raider.
Shindongbang also urged the retailer to hold a shareholders' meeting to question what it described as lax management.
Shindongbang, with its joint venture Dongbang Peregrine Securities, holds a 6.74 percent stake in Midopa.
"Our stance on wanting to participate in Midopa's management has not changed," Kim Jin-il, a Shindongbang director told Reuters.

"Shindongbang's requests to the court means the company will push forward with its takeover attempt, regardless of the federation's warning," said Joo Han, head of mergers and acquistions at LG Securities.
"Noboby can block Shindongbang if it really wants to take over Midopa," said Kim Min-tae, an economist at Daewoo Research and Economic Institute.

Brokers said the combined shareholding by Shindongbang and others friendly to it was about 38 percent, while Dainong Corp, the parent company of Midopa, earlier said it and its friendly forces held a combined 40 percent stake.
Shindongbang has said it would accumulate more shares in Midopa through tender offers, although a final decision and details have not yet been prepared.
Shindongbang startled the stock market last week when it told the exchange it was considering taking over Midopa.
Korea Industrial Co, whose president is a brother of the chairman of Shindongbang, said it was also thinking of making a bid for the retailer.
Neither company has announced a final decision.
Hostile takeovers are virtually unheard of in South Korea, although new rules that came into effect in January make them possible. Many still believed the concept was unethical.
The federation, representing the interests of the nation's large conglomerates or "chaebol", urged Shindongbang and Dainong to compromise.
But Shindongbang's Kim said: "Chances that both parties can settle the issue through compromise look bleak."
He denied news reports that the chairmen of Shindongbang and Dainong met to settle the takeover issue.
Shindongbang asked a Seoul court this week to prevent Midopa from issuing equity-linked bonds, which analysts said would be one way for Midopa to defend itself from a takeover bid.
Shindongbang added it asked the court to nullify last Friday's issuance by Midopa of 50 billion won ($56.96 million) worth of bonds with warrants and the exercising rights by underwriters.
Institutional investors affiliated with the Samsung Group, Hyundai and LG, bought all of the bonds. They are entitled to convert the bonds into Midopa shares from July.
Midopa shares ended on Thursday 2,300 won lower at 27,600, the fourth consecutive fall in a row. (Conversion $ = 877.80)
